This vignette walks through a complete analysis of one synthetic study,
`master_synthetic_data`, which has every column the package uses. It ships with
the package and is the dashboard's "All Features" demo.

```{r library}
library(mouseExperiment)
m <- master_synthetic_data
str(m)
table(m$Treatment)
```

Six arms of 8 mice each sit in two cages per arm: a vehicle control, a Drug_A
dose series (low, mid and high), Drug_B, and the combination of Drug_A Mid with
Drug_B. Mice are measured every two days until day 26, or until they are removed
at the tumour volume endpoint (`Survival_Censor = 1` on their last row).

# From a study file to volumes and study days

The study already carries `Volume` and `Day`. Raw laboratory data usually has
calendar dates and caliper measurements instead, as the combination study's file
does. The preparation functions read and convert it, in this order; the
dashboard uses the same functions, and its R script replays them:

* `read_study_csv()` reads a CSV with comma, semicolon or tab separators, a
  decimal comma, and UTF-8, Latin-1 or UTF-16 text;
* `apply_exclusions()` removes animals, arms or cages you leave out;
* `label_cages()` makes cage labels unique when cages are numbered within each
  arm (below);
* `study_days()` turns dates into study days, letting the whole column decide
  whether 03/04 is the 3rd of April or the 4th of March;
* `calculate_volume()` turns caliper measurements into volumes;
* `label_arms()` labels each arm by treatment and dose, and
  `survival_events()` reduces the data to one row per animal for survival.

```{r prepare}
path <- system.file("sample_data", "combo_treatment_synthetic_data.csv",
                    package = "mouseExperiment")
raw <- read_study_csv(path)
head(raw, 3)
d <- study_days(raw, date_column = "Date", reference_date = "2025-03-24")
d <- calculate_volume(d)          # ellipsoid: pi * L * W^2 / 6
head(d[, c("Treatment", "Cage", "ID", "Day", "Volume")], 3)
```

When every date has one known format, `calculate_dates()` reads them with it.

`calculate_volume()` also offers the modified ellipsoid, cylinder, sphere, box
and a three-axis ellipsoid when a height is measured
(`height_column = "Height"`).

A cage label is read as one cage. These data label their cages across the
study, 1 to 4. If yours are numbered within each arm, C1 and C2 in every arm,
make the labels unique first, or each label is read as one cage holding every
arm:

```{r cages}
cages <- data.frame(Treatment = rep(c("Vehicle", "Drug_A"), each = 2),
                    Cage = c("C1", "C2", "C1", "C2"))
label_cages(cages)$Cage
```

# Which days can be compared

Once mice start leaving at the endpoint, late days compare survivors only. An
arm is evaluable on a day while at least half of its enrolled animals, and at
least three, are still on study. Endpoint-based summaries such as tumour growth
inhibition (TGI) and synergy use only those days.

```{r evaluable}
ev <- evaluable_days(m, volume_column = "Volume")
ev$rule
ev$last_day
```

# Tumour growth

```{r growth-plot}
plot_tumor_growth(m, necrotic_column = "Necrotic")
```

`tumor_growth_statistics()` fits a linear mixed model to log volume, with
correlated random intercepts and slopes per animal by default. It falls back to
simpler structures, with a warning, when the data cannot support them. Tests are
Type III F-tests with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, and comparisons are
against the reference group.

```{r growth-stats}
tg <- tumor_growth_statistics(m, reference_group = "Vehicle",
                              p_adjust_method = "holm")
tg$random_effects
tg$anova
tg$pairwise_comparisons
```

Per-animal growth rates, and the fixed effects with their intervals:

```{r growth-plots}
plot_growth_rate(tg$growth_rates, error_bar_type = "CI")
plot_caterpillar(tg$model, show_intercept = FALSE)
```

`tumor_doubling_time()` reports doubling times per animal, and
`trajectory_permutation_test()` gives a permutation test of whole trajectories
at the declared unit of randomisation (`perm_spec(unit = "mouse")` or
`"cage"`).

# Drug synergy

Bliss independence compares the combination's growth inhibition with what two
independently acting drugs would give. The verdict depends on the interval of
the Bliss difference, not on its point estimate.

```{r synergy}
syn <- analyze_drug_synergy(m,
  drug_a_name = "Drug_A Mid", drug_b_name = "Drug_B",
  combo_name = "Drug_A Mid + Drug_B", reference_group = "Vehicle",
  cage_column = "Cage", n_boot = 500, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
syn$summary
plot_drug_synergy(syn)
```

The same comparison on every evaluable day:

```{r synergy-trend}
trend <- analyze_drug_synergy_over_time(m,
  drug_a_name = "Drug_A Mid", drug_b_name = "Drug_B",
  combo_name = "Drug_A Mid + Drug_B", reference_group = "Vehicle",
  min_day = 2, cage_column = "Cage", n_boot = 500, seed = 1,
  verbose = FALSE)
plot_synergy_trend(trend)
```

# Dose-response

Dose-response analyses one agent's dose series against its control.

```{r dose}
dr <- dose_response_statistics(m,
  treatments = c("Drug_A Low", "Drug_A Mid", "Drug_A High"),
  reference_group = "Vehicle", cage_column = "Cage", verbose = FALSE)
dr$summary_table
dr$trend_test
```

# Survival

Survival needs one row per animal, with its time and event.
`survival_events()` makes it. It keys animals by arm, ID and cage, so ear tags
reused in each arm stay apart, and an event is at the animal's first flagged
day. With `volume_limit` instead of `event_column`, an event is the first day
a tumour reached that volume. Here the unit of randomisation is the mouse.
With `randomisation_unit = "cage"` the comparison becomes a cage-level
permutation log-rank test instead.

```{r survival}
per_animal <- survival_events(m, event_column = "Survival_Censor",
                              cage_column = "Cage")
surv <- survival_statistics(per_animal, time_column = "Time",
                            event_column = "Event", reference_group = "Vehicle",
                            verbose = FALSE)
surv$method_used
surv$results
```

Two arms (Drug_A High and the combination) have no events, so an ordinary Cox
model has no finite estimate for them. `coxph` says so in its warning. The
hazard ratios reported come from Firth's penalised likelihood
(`method_used = "coxphf"`), which stays finite with zero events.

# Body weight and the therapeutic window

Body weight is modelled with the tumour's own mass subtracted
(`adjust_tumor_weight = TRUE`). That needs the volume units, so they are
declared rather than guessed.

```{r weight}
bw <- analyze_body_weight(m, volume_column = "Volume", volume_units = "mm3",
                          cage_column = "Cage", reference_group = "Vehicle")
bw$pairwise_comparisons
```

The therapeutic window puts efficacy (model-based TGI at the last evaluable
day) beside tolerability (each arm's worst weight loss from its own baseline),
each with an interval:

```{r window}
tw <- therapeutic_window_metric(m, volume_units = "mm3", cage_column = "Cage",
                                reference_group = "Vehicle",
                                n_boot = 500, seed = 1)
tw$window_table
```

# Planning the next study

```{r power}
# Animals per group for a standardised effect of 1.2, three groups
apriori_power_analysis(effect_size = 1.2, n_groups = 3)
```

`apriori_power_simulation()` simulates whole studies with the same mixed model,
including random slopes and dropout at a volume limit. Use at least 500
simulations in practice.

# The dashboard and its R script

`run_dashboard()` opens the same analyses in a browser, without code. Each tab's
**Download Results** offers a ZIP of the tables, plots, diagnostics and data,
an HTML report, and an R script that reruns the analysis with these functions.
The script starts from the analysed data, or, with "Include my original file"
ticked, from the file you uploaded: it replays the preparation above with the
settings you chose, and stops unless the result is the data the dashboard
analysed.

# Bayesian models

`bayesian_tumor_growth()` and `bayesian_survival()` fit the Bayesian versions of
the growth model and the survival model with brms. Priors are scaled to the
data, and their strength is chosen with `prior_strength` or `tg_priors()`. The
first fit compiles a Stan model, which takes about 30 seconds; later fits with
the same structure reuse it.

```{r bayes, eval = FALSE}
two_arms <- subset(m, Treatment %in% c("Vehicle", "Drug_A High"))
fit <- bayesian_tumor_growth(two_arms, cage_column = "Cage",
                             priors = tg_priors(strength = "weakly_informative"),
                             mcmc = tg_mcmc(chains = 4, iter = 1000))
fit$treatment_effects
```
